title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6797 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: India October CPI inflation rises to 6.09%, food inflation accelerates to 8.94%
body: India CPI Y/Y 6.09% vs 5.93% expected Prior 5.54% Full report India's CPI rose to 6.09% y/y in October, according to provisional data, pointing to increased price pressures in the economy. The headline inflation rate was higher in rural areas, where prices increased by 6.63% y/y, compared with 5.41% in urban areas. Food inflation was a big standout, with the Consumer Food Price Index rising 8.94% y/y in October. Food price increases were relatively broad-based across the country, with rural food inflation reaching 9.09% and urban food inflation standing at 8.68%. The figures highlight the significant contribution of food prices to India's inflationary pressures, with food inflation running well above the headline CPI rate. Overall, the October report points to a challenging inflation environment for the Reserve Bank of India. Given the acceleration in inflation, the market is pricing in a 69% chance of a 25 bps hike at the next RBI meeting, with 31% probabilitiy of a larger 50 bps move. The US-Iran war has been a major contributor of inflation through higher crude oil prices, increasing India's import bill and raising transportation, energy and agricultural production costs. As a major oil importer, India is particularly vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the Middle East. Higher energy and fertiliser costs gradually feed into consumer prices, while a weaker rupee also makes imports more expensive. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Crude oil is caught between hopes of de-escalation and concerns of further escalation. What's next?
body: Crude oil has been consolidating around recent lows as the US-Iran uncertainty keeps traders guessing on the next move. The US-Iran conflict remains the main driver of course, with diplomatic efforts showing some signs of progress but no concrete breakthrough yet. Oil prices dipped yesterday after the Wall Street Journal reported that the US Vice President Vance was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official in an effort to end the war. However, significant mistrust remains, with Iranian officials accusing Washington of preparing further military strikes or tighter economic pressure. Iran has also continued to issue warnings of retaliation against US military bases and reportedly targeted ship navigation systems near the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the US military says its blockade has prevented Iran from exporting oil, while US forces are working to keep the Strait open to commercial shipping. The conflicting signals leave the outlook highly uncertain, with oil prices remaining sensitive to any developments that could either pave the way for de-escalation or trigger another escalation. It goes without saying that a concrete breakthrough would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly.

title: Chart of the day: USD/JPY nears 160.00 as technical warning signs raise Japan intervention risks
body: Well, it looks like dollar bulls are starting to play with fire again. USD/JPY is creeping back towards the 160.00 level and while the move might look like another show of strength for the dollar, I suspect that Japanese authorities aren't finding it quite as amusing. And from a technical perspective, there are reasons why Tokyo officials might be getting a tad bit nervous this week. After spending much of October repeatedly struggling to really test the 159.00 level and with repeated failed attempts in getting above the 200-day moving average (blue line), USD/JPY has finally pushed past those key resistance levels. Buyers had been knocking on the same door for weeks but are now finally managing a breakthrough. And with price pushing past both the key daily moving averages in the latest run higher, the technical picture is threatening to open up towards 160.00 next. However, this is where things start to get a little more dicey for USD/JPY and dollar bulls. The 160.00 mark isn't just another technical level. These sort of big psychological barriers and figure levels are often a potential trigger point for Japanese authorities to step up their intervention warnings or even potentially act outright. This was precisely where we saw intervention action back during late April and early May. And with USD/JPY now approaching that territory again, the technical break above 159.00 provides a rather clear reason for Tokyo officials to worry about the yen's renewed depreciation.

title: Bitcoin consolidates near recent lows as hawkish Fed repricing weighs on the crypto market
body: Bitcoin has been mostly consolidating around recent lows as the hawkish repricing triggered by Fed governor Waller's remarks and the hot US CPI weighed on the crypto market. As a reminder, Fed's Waller not only said he would support a rate hike in December regardless of the inflation data but also raised the possibility of a larger 50 bps move if inflation comes in hotter than expected. Sure enough, the US CPI data came in above expectations and increased the probabilities of 50 bps hike. Following the CPI data, Fed's Hammack also left a door open for a larger rate increase. Traders are currently pricing in just a 12% probability of a 50 bps hike, but those odds could climb further if more Fed officials endorse the possibility or refrain from pushing back against it. Meanwhile, US-Iran negotiations remain in a deadlock. The WSJ reported that US Vice President Vance is considering holding face-to-face talks with a senior Iranian security official in an attempt to bring the conflict to an end. However, separate reports suggested that senior Iranian officials believe Washington is preparing either further military strikes or tighter economic pressure in an attempt to provoke a response from Tehran. There is clearly still a significant amount of mistrust between the two sides, reinforcing the view that a diplomatic breakthrough may not be as near as market expected. Looking ahead, Bitcoin will likely remain under pressure amid the negative macro backdrop.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran negotiations remain at a stalemate. The central bank's resident dove is once again preaching caution, warning that further tightening could undermine the progress that Japan has made in achieving sustainable inflation. Here are his latest remarks from today: Inflation has already reached roughly 2%, leaving little reason to push prices higher BOJ must be cautious about raising interest rates too quickly Further rate hikes may be necessary in the future, but should be carried out slowly Not opposed to raising rates altogether and is not considering proposing a rate cut Japan's neutral interest rate may be somewhat above the current policy rate Has no specific terminal interest rate in mind Policy decisions should be assessed at every meeting, considering economic risks and financial conditions BOJ could still raise or lower rates even after reaching a level consistent with its inflation target BOJ does not directly control exchange rates (declines to specify a desirable USD/JPY level) Further tightening risks weakening underlying inflation, particularly as consumption continues to lack momentum Now, I wouldn't read too much into the dovish undertones here. title: Chinese tech firms reportedly rushing to secure more Nvidia chip capacity amid fears that spy scandal would spur tighter restrictions
body: Well, talk about a scandal sending everyone scrambling for the exits. Except in this case, Chinese tech firms aren't exactly looking to leave the party. Instead, they're trying to grab as much Nvidia computing power as they can before Washington potentially slams the door shut. Reuters is reporting that AI companies in China are looking to secure more Nvidia-powered cloud computing capacity at overseas data centres, fearing that the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang could accelerate tougher US restrictions, citing three people familiar with the matter. The sources noted that a major Chinese cloud provider has reportedly discussed locking in overseas capacity, while smaller AI firms are exploring similar arrangements - particularly in Southeast Asia. And there's good reason that Chinese tech firms are getting nervous here. For some context, the US already restricts China's access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips. However, these companies have been able to work around some of those restrictions by renting computing power from data centres outside the country. The fear now is that at some point, that very loophole could soon become a casualty of the latest political fallout. Essentially, Huang's latest affair scandal and controversy with a woman who is suspected to be a Chinese spy has given lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for tighter export controls.

title: Heads up: UK September GDP in focus but will weak growth really stop the BOE from hiking again?
body: The UK September monthly and latest quarterly GDP report are due at 0700 GMT today and the question that markets will be asking is just how bad would the numbers have to be to convince the BOE to take its foot off the rate hike pedal? The estimates are pointing to a flat reading after the economy expanded by just 0.1% in August. And that follows from the more encouraging 0.4% increase in July, suggesting that growth momentum is becoming rather uneven in the past quarter. That being said, the bigger picture isn't quite as soft as the latest monthly numbers might suggest. The UK economy expanded by 0.7% in the three months to August, largely supported by services activity. Meanwhile, manufacturing and construction have also been keeping pace, albeit less convincingly. Besides the monthly figures, we'll also be getting the preliminary Q3 GDP estimate. So, that should ffer a better sense of whether the economy is holding up or starting to buckle under the weight of higher borrowing costs and surging energy prices. The latter have seen some better developments in the past week but will still need time to filter through back to the economy. At the balance, a downside surprise in the numbers could weigh on sterling and temper expectations for further BOE tightening. But unless we see a particularly ugly set of numbers, I reckon that today's report will do little to materially change up the BOE's plans for December at this juncture.

That matters most for USD/JPY, which is already near the 160 area where Japan has stepped up verbal warnings. Higher long-end yields would also weigh on gold, which has slipped below $4,000, and add pressure on richly valued tech stocks already hit by the Nvidia leadership shock. Oil is the key risk to the call. A sustained fall in crude would ease inflation fears and could cap yields, while a renewed rise linked to the Iran war would reinforce the move higher. --- Cheaper oil might give Treasuries a breather, but CBA thinks growth and a hawkish Fed will keep pushing the 10-year yield higher. title: ANZ says RBA hike bets have cooled, but 3.7% core inflation will keep it cautious
body: Cooler RBA hike expectations take away one source of support for the Australian dollar, at a time when US yields are rising and the Fed is on a hiking path. That leaves the AUD exposed to further dollar strength. Sticky services inflation should limit how far Australian rate expectations can fall, though, which caps the downside for front-end bond yields. Lower oil prices help Australian headline inflation but do little for the domestic services pressures ANZ is focused on, so the RBA's cautious stance looks likely to persist. --- Growth is cooling, but services inflation isn't, and that keeps the RBA from relaxing even as the case for another hike fades.
